extracted.intended_audience: Inhabitants of America (American colonists / general public)
extracted.subtask_description: A persuasive 1776 pamphlet arguing for American independence, criticizing monarchy and hereditary succession, and prescribing principles for government (simplicity, security, representation) and for persuasive political writing (plain arguments, avoidance of personal attacks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Design and end of government: security with least expense
rubrics_metrics.description: "Wherefore, security being the true design and end of government, it unanswerably follows that whatever form thereof appears most likely to ensure it to us, with the least expence and greatest benefit, is preferable to all others."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate forms of government by whether they ensure security and do so with minimal cost and maximal benefit to the people. Prefer the form that best secures liberty and safety while minimizing burdens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity principle for government forms
rubrics_metrics.description: "I draw my idea of the form of government from a principle in nature, which no art can overturn, viz. that the more simple any thing is, the less liable it is to be disordered; and the easier repaired when disordered."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor simpler governmental structures because simplicity reduces disorder and makes failures easier to remedy. Complexity is criticized as making faults hard to locate and cure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequent elections to maintain representatives' fidelity
rubrics_metrics.description: "...prudence will point out the propriety of having elections often; because ... their fidelity to the public will be secured by the prudent reflexion of not making a rod for themselves."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use frequent, regular elections so elected officials frequently return to and mix with the electors, preventing the formation of a separate governing interest and encouraging accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportional/divided representation as population grows
rubrics_metrics.description: "If the colony continue increasing, it will become necessary to augment the number of the representatives, and that the interest of every part of the colony may be attended to, it will be found best to divide the whole into convenient parts, each part sending its proper number;"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As population and geographic dispersion increase, expand the number of representatives and divide constituencies into convenient parts so all local interests are attended to.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representatives should act as whole body would act
rubrics_metrics.description: "...leave the legislative part to be managed by a select number chosen from the whole body, who are supposed to have the same concerns at stake which those who appointed them, and who will act in the same manner as the whole body would act were they present."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislators' legitimacy depends on representing the interests and expected actions of the whole electorate, not forming separate or self-interested factions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government arises from human wickedness; society from wants
rubrics_metrics.description: "Society is produced by our wants, and government by our wickedness; the former promotes our happiness positively ... the latter negatively by restraining our vices."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat government as a necessary corrective to human vice rather than as a wholly positive creation; this frames expectations about limits and purposes of political authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid personal attacks in persuasive political writing
rubrics_metrics.description: "In the following sheets, the author hath studiously avoided every thing which is personal among ourselves. Compliments as well as censure to individuals make no part thereof."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing political argument, emphasize ideas and principles rather than targeting individuals; maintain a focus on doctrine over personalities to preserve persuasiveness and broad appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use plain facts, plain arguments, and common sense
rubrics_metrics.description: "In the following pages I offer nothing more than simple facts, plain arguments, and common sense;"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer straightforward language, clear facts, and commonsense reasoning for maximum persuasive power with a general audience; avoid abstruse technicalities that alienate readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex constitutions reduce accountability and foster corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: "The constitution of England is so exceedingly complex, that the nation may suffer for years together without being able to discover in which part the fault lies..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware constitutions or systems so complex that cause-and-effect are obscured; complexity can mask the seat of power and enable patronage and corruption (e.g., crown giving places and pensions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of monarchy and hereditary succession
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple passages argue monarchy is unjust, idolatrous, and harmful: e.g., "Monarchy is ranked in scripture as one of the sins of the Jews..." and hereditary succession "is an insult and an imposition on posterity."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess monarchy/hereditary succession on moral and practical grounds: they unjustly elevate some by birth, invite unworthy rulers, foster corruption, and historically produce war and civil strife rather than lasting peace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patronage (places and pensions) as source of crown power
rubrics_metrics.description: "...it derives its whole consequence merely from being the giver of places and pensions... though we have been wise enough to shut and lock a door against absolute monarchy, we at the same time have been foolish enough to put the crown in possession of the key."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize distribution of offices and pensions as a key mechanism by which executive power is extended and legislative independence eroded; evaluate systems for vulnerabilities to patronage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public sanction as initial enforcement for new societies
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is more than probable that their first laws will have the title only of Regulations, and be enforced by no other penalty than public disesteem."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In early or small societies, rely initially on social norms and public disesteem to enforce regulations before establishing harsher legal penalties; social enforcement can sustain compliance when institutions are informal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continental union and permanence of consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: "The sun never shined on a cause of greater worth... 'Tis not the concern of a day... posterity are virtually involved in the contest... Now is the seed time of continental union, faith and honor."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating political action, consider long-term and continental-level consequences; prioritize durable union and principles that will affect posterity rather than short-term compromises.
